title: Funds, ETFs and Index Investing
intro: A fund pools money from many investors and buys a portfolio on their behalf. Funds give small investors diversification, professional management and low trading costs; they are how most people should own stocks and bonds. The choice that matters most is not which manager is cleverest but how much you pay and how broadly you diversify.

items: Mutual funds (in the UK, unit trusts and OEICs): bought and sold directly with the fund company once a day at the net asset value (NAV), the value of the holdings per share computed after the market closes.

Exchange-traded funds (ETFs): fund shares that trade on an exchange all day like a stock. Authorized participants (large dealers) create and redeem ETF shares in exchange for baskets of the underlying securities, which keeps the ETF price close to its NAV. The first US ETF, the SPDR S&P 500 (SPY), launched in 1993.

Index funds: mutual funds or ETFs that hold an index's securities in index weights rather than picking. John Bogle's Vanguard launched the first retail index fund in 1976 (mocked at the time as 'Bogle's folly').
Actively managed funds: a manager picks securities trying to beat a benchmark.
Closed-end funds and investment trusts: a fixed number of shares that trade on an exchange, often at a discount or premium to NAV. They can use leverage and hold illiquid assets.

Money market funds: hold T-bills, repo and very short high-grade debt and aim to keep a stable \$1.00 price. In 2008 the Reserve Primary Fund 'broke the buck' after its Lehman Brothers paper defaulted, so government-only money funds are the safest kind.
Target-date funds: a single fund that holds a stock-and-bond mix and shifts toward bonds as a set retirement year approaches (its glide path). The default option in many US 401(k) plans.

Hedge funds and private funds: for wealthy or institutional investors, with fewer rules, high fees (traditionally '2 and 20': 2% of assets plus 20% of profits) and limited ability to withdraw. See Real Estate, Commodities and Alternatives.

blocks.text: The expense ratio is the yearly fee as a share of your money, taken quietly from the fund's assets. Broad index ETFs charge around 0.03 to 0.10%; the average actively managed stock fund charges several times that, and some funds still add a sales load (an up-front or exit commission) or a 12b-1 marketing fee. On top come costs that never appear in the expense ratio: trading costs inside the fund (higher for funds with high turnover), cash drag, and taxes on distributed gains.

William Sharpe's arithmetic of active management (1991) explains why costs decide the contest. Before costs, the average actively managed dollar must earn the market return, because active and passive investors together hold the market and the passive ones earn exactly its return. After costs, which are higher for active management, the average active dollar must therefore trail the average passive dollar. This is arithmetic, not a theory about markets being efficient.

The evidence agrees. S&P's SPIVA scorecards report that over 15-year periods roughly 85 to 95% of US large-cap active funds have trailed the S&P 500, with similar results in most categories and countries. And past winners rarely stay winners: S&P's persistence scorecards find that top-quartile funds are no more likely than chance to remain in the top quartile a few years later. Fees, by contrast, are persistent and are one of the best predictors of future fund returns (Morningstar has found this repeatedly).

widget.title: What a fee costs over time

blocks.text: A rule of thumb: over 30 years each 0.1% of yearly fee costs about 3% of the final balance. A 1% fee costs about a quarter of it.

items: Market-cap weighting (most indexes) needs little trading and holds every stock in proportion to its size, so it is the only way all investors together can hold the market. Its weakness is concentration in whatever has become most valuable.
Equal weighting gives every company the same weight, tilting toward smaller companies and requiring more trading.

Fundamental and factor ('smart beta') indexes weight by sales, dividends, value, momentum, quality or low volatility. They are active bets packaged as indexes; see Portfolio Theory for the evidence on factors.
Tracking error is how much a fund's return differs from its index; tracking difference is the average gap, usually close to the expense ratio. Securities lending income can make it smaller.

ETFs trade intraday, have no minimums, and in the US are usually more tax-efficient: in-kind redemptions let them hand away low-cost-basis shares without selling, so they rarely distribute capital gains.
Mutual funds allow automatic investing of exact amounts and avoid bid-ask spreads; for index mutual funds at low-cost firms the difference is small.

Watch out for leveraged and inverse ETFs (2× or 3× the daily move, or −1×). Because they reset daily, their long-run return is not 2× or 3× the index's; in volatile markets they can lose money even when the index rises. They are trading tools, not holdings.
Thematic ETFs (a hot technology, a trend) tend to launch after the theme has done well and have often underperformed after launch.

widget.title: Leveraged daily funds: compound return against volatility

blocks.text: The plot uses the approximation $g_L \approx L\mu - (L - 1)r_b - f - L^2\sigma^2/2$: the volatility drag grows with the square of the leverage. At 25% volatility the 3× fund's drag is about 28% a year, which swamps its tripled average return. (Fees of about 0.9% are assumed for the 2× and 3× funds.)

items: What does it hold? Read the index or mandate, the top holdings and the sector and country weights.
What does it cost? Expense ratio, loads, and for ETFs the typical bid-ask spread.
How big and how old is it? Tiny funds close; a long record shows how it tracks.
How tax-efficient is it, if held in a taxable account?
Does it overlap with what you already own? Three US large-cap funds are one fund three times.

blocks.text: A widely used simple setup is a three-fund portfolio: a total home-market stock index fund, a total international stock index fund and a total bond index fund, in proportions that match your risk tolerance, or a single target-date or balanced fund that does the same.

blocks.title: Fee drag
blocks.text: \$100,000 grows for 25 years at 7% a year before fees. Compare the ending balance in a fund charging 0.05% and one charging 1.2% (fees taken yearly from the return).
solution: $100000 \times 1.058^{25} \approx \$409{,}000$. The higher fee costs about \$127,000, almost a quarter of the cheaper fund's result.

blocks.title: Sharpe's arithmetic
blocks.text: Passive investors own 50% of a market that returns 8% in a year. Passive funds cost 0.05% and active funds average 0.8% in fees and trading costs. What did the average passive and average active dollar earn?
solution: Before costs both earn 8%, since together they hold the market and the passive half earns exactly the market. After costs, the passive dollar earns 7.95% and the average active dollar 7.2%.

blocks.title: Leveraged ETF decay
blocks.text: An index goes up 10% one day and down 9.09% the next, ending where it started. What happens to a 3× daily fund?
solution: Day 1: $+30\% \Rightarrow 1.30$. Day 2: $-27.27\% \Rightarrow 1.30 \times 0.7273 \approx 0.9455$. The fund is down about 5.5% though the index is flat. Repeated, this drag compounds.
